examples.title: Two squares, one royal swap
examples.text: Thirty-two pieces on a glossy vinyl board, seen at an angle. Sixty-two squares are right; the two that are not are d8 and e8, where the black queen and king — standing shoulder to shoulder — are read as each other. Naming the two tallest pieces apart on a crowded back rank is what remains of this problem — and a swap is the one version of it that checking the material cannot catch, since each side still has one queen and one king.

examples.title: A clean read
examples.text: The opening position after 1.b4 d5. All 64 squares correct, including the knight on b1 half hidden behind its rook — the square the previous model misnamed from this angle. Every piece found, every piece named.

examples.title: The back rank, where the tall pieces stand together
examples.text: Two wrong squares, both on the first rank: the queen on d1 is called a king, and the king on e1 shrinks to a pawn behind its neighbours. The bishop on f1, which a single look at the photograph called a rook, now comes back right. A crowded back rank seen from low down is the hardest thing on the board — queen and king read as each other is still the most common mistake in the whole split.

examples.title: Read from the wrong end
examples.text: One of the two worst boards in the split, and the pieces are not the problem: turn this answer around and it scores 64 of 64. Eight pieces on an almost empty board leave very little evidence for the last step, deciding which corner is a8, and it went the wrong way. The other is the same failure tipped by one missed pawn. Nothing else in 306 photographs is wrong by more than four squares.
